#24226. Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports WebAuthn redirection

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (263 w)

Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports WebAuthn redirection

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (263 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports WebAuthn redirection, so users can sign in to websites and applications in their streaming session with a FIDO2 authenticator on their local device, such as a security key, Windows Hello, or Touch ID.
  • Sources indicate that when an application in the session makes a WebAuthn request, WorkSpaces Applications forwards it to the user's device, where the authenticator signs it and returns the response.
  • WebAuthn redirection is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions where WorkSpaces Applications is available.

Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports WebAuthn redirection, so users can sign in to websites and applications in their streaming session with a FIDO2 authenticator on their local device, such as a security key, Windows Hello, or Touch ID. Previously, an authenticator attached to the user's computer was not available inside the streaming session, so organizations that require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) had to use weaker sign-in methods or keep those applications off WorkSpaces Applications. This helps organizations with FIDO2 requirements stream those applications.

Sources indicate that when an application in the session makes a WebAuthn request, WorkSpaces Applications forwards it to the user's device, where the authenticator signs it and returns the response. Private keys never leave the user's device. Administrators turn it on per stack in the console or API, and on Windows fleets can limit it to an allow list of processes. For example, a bank can let employees sign in to Microsoft 365 in their streaming session with the same security key they use on their laptop.

WebAuthn redirection is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions where WorkSpaces Applications is available.

To get started, select Enable WebAuthn redirection under User Settings for your stack, use an image with the WorkSpaces Applications agent released on or after October 20, 2026, and connect with the WorkSpaces Applications client for Windows (1.5.0 or later) or macOS (1.6.0 or later). To learn more, see WebAuthn redirection in the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications Administration Guide, or visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications product page.

#24224. Industry News: Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

Industry News: Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui.
  • Industry observers note that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes.
  • You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Industry observers note that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

Recent findings suggest that in Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

Sources indicate that that same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

According to recent reports, the drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

It has been revealed that this is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

Sources indicate that this is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Industry observers note that background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Recent findings suggest that canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

There are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

It has been revealed that AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

According to recent reports, the image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

Recent findings suggest that so far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

Sources indicate that A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:.

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

Recent findings suggest that this isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

In a recent development, every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node shows up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:.

Industry observers note that now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:.

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

In a recent development, if you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Recent findings suggest that whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

Industry observers note that really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes.

It has been revealed that analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

Evidence sufficiency assessment enables cost-effective review allocation in on-premise clinical AI agents

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (163 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.27390v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: On-premise clinical AI agents must auto-accept high-confidence diagnoses, deferring others to clinician review, yet token probabilities and self-reported confidence miss errors, while more reliable five-run consistency incurs fivefold compute. We propose training-free decision-point evidence sufficiency assessment and a three-tier sequential triage protocol. Masking reasoning and diagnosis, the same 4B model scores sufficiency from objective evidence via prior-debiased probabilities over five ordered levels. Calibration freezes a nominal top-50% threshold, selecting single-run, five-run consistency, or full-deferral tiers by whether the one-sided 95% Wilson lower confidence bound of pass rate among accepted cases meets the 95% clinical target line. Across 1,605 MIRA-v2, CDM, VivaBench, and in-hospital liver malignancy primary cohort cases, MIRA-v2 single-run top-50% pass rate reached 98.91%, matching five-run consistency, saving ~80% compute; CDM achieved 96.00% test attainment by escalating to the five-run consistency tier; cross-specialty, missing-imaging, and combined enriched cohorts entered the full-deferral tier, capping calibration false-certification rate at 0.00%-3.50%.

Tech Report: How Vodafone is using the Data Engineering Agent to improve their data pipelines

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manager, Data & Analytics Engineering, Vodafone.
  • For large organizations, building and maintaining data pipelines is one of the most complex tasks that data engineering teams are tasked with.
  • In this blog post, Vodafone Czech Republic describes how it has used the Data Engineering Agent to modernize and optimize BigQuery stored procedures, transforming them into modern data pipelines and reducing pipeline execution times by half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sr. Manager, Data & Analytics Engineering, Vodafone.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

For large organizations, building and maintaining data pipelines is one of the most complex tasks that data engineering teams are tasked with. In BigQuery environments, the Data Engineering Agent can help, leveraging Gemini to to automate these workflows.

In this blog post, Vodafone Czech Republic describes how it has used the Data Engineering Agent to modernize and optimize BigQuery stored procedures, transforming them into modern data pipelines and reducing pipeline execution times by half. - Pedro Esteves, Google Cloud.

According to recent reports, the Data Engineering Agent makes it easy to build and maintain modern data pipelines. The agent is available in BigQuery pipelines and Dataform. At Vodafone, we used the agent directly in Dataform to build Dataform pipelines. As shown in the example below, the Data Engineering Agent takes natural language instructions together with any code provided in the instruction file to build the Dataform pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that vodafone Czech Republic uses many BigQuery stored procedures to transform data for business purposes. These stored procedures are a legacy of a previous on-premises data warehouse migration to BigQuery. Many of them contain 2,000 or 3,000 lines of code and run sequentially.

Compared to a modular Dataform approach created by the Data Engineering Agent, there are several known disadvantages of maintaining legacy, multi-thousand-line stored procedures, as described in the table below.

Legacy stored procedures (Monolith).

Single file, 1000s of lines, complex logic mixed.

Copy/Paste code blocks (prone to drift).

functions and ref() for strict logic reuse.

Automated testing (Unique, Not Null, Referential Integrity) built-in.

Comments in code (usually outdated).

Auto-generated documentation with lineage graph.

Manual scheduling; hard-coded dependency management.

Automatic execution based on lineage (DAG).

To solve the problems of running and maintaining legacy stored procedures, we used the Data Engineering Agent to migrate some of the stored procedures into Dataform pipelines.

Recent findings suggest that the Data Engineering Agent was able to parallelize the code into independent steps which are then run in parallel to improve readability and performance. See the example below:.

Sources indicate that the Data Engineering Agent can understand dependencies between the tables and cache certain intermediate tables using BigQuery materialized views. This means that tables that are used in downstream processes can be cached, speeding up code execution and reducing cost.

Industry observers note that having a modular pipeline allows us to facilitate end-to-end orchestration and pipeline dependencies to meet our SLAs. Before using Dataform, we had to manually control pipeline execution by creating metadata tables with several checkpoints and logs. Dependencies between stored procedures jobs were also maintained manually in a spreadsheet. By executing the pipeline in Dataform, all the dependencies and execution logs are handled by Dataform.

It has been revealed that because the code is now split into several steps, it’s possible to execute only a subset of the actions in Dataform rather than running the entire stored procedure. This can help with debugging and gives us the flexibility to only run the relevant sections of the code.

There’s a trade-off between parallelization and caching. When we prompted the Data Engineering Agent to parallelize our procedures, we noticed an increase in cost.

When running a standard sequential stored procedure, BigQuery caches the base table for the first thread. However, splitting this logic into parallel streams can inadvertently negate those caching benefits, causing full table scans for each thread.

To solve this, we asked the Data Engineering Agent to create materialized views for intermediate tables. These views effectively pre-cache the data, ensuring that your parallelized queries remain performant and cost-efficient.

To make the agent parallelize the code more efficiently we gave it specific instructions on which areas (staging tables) we were interested in parallelizing.

Industry observers note that deploying Data Engineering Agent delivered immediate and measurable impact, specifically in addressing the toil associated with legacy migrations. The agent successfully achieved high-fidelity replication of all stored procedures, ensuring 1:1 logic parity with minimal human intervention.

According to recent reports, by automating the conversion of complex ETL pipelines, the agent achieved a 90% reduction in migration time compared with traditional manual approaches. What would have typically required weeks of engineering effort was completed in a fraction of the time, freeing engineers to focus on other key tasks.

Furthermore, the modernization of the underlying infrastructure resulted in substantial performance gains. Post-migration benchmarks indicate that the fresh data pipelines run twice as fast, significantly reducing query latency and increasing overall data throughput.

And as we previously discussed, instructing the agent to cache intermediate tables led to a 30% reduction in costs.

Beyond accelerating development and reducing costs, these agentic tools are also changing the way data engineers approach their work. Rather than spending significant time on repetitive migration and optimization tasks, engineers can collaborate with agents to explore different implementation options, validate design decisions, and accelerate delivery. This shift is encouraging teams to adopt new ways of working, where agentic capabilities become an integral part of the development process and help shape how data solutions are designed, delivered, and maintained.

At Vodafone, we’re planning to scale the use of the Data Engineering Agent across the manufacturer in the following key areas:.

Standardized Dataform template repository: Establishing a central repository for Dataform templates allows for consistent architecture and design patterns across different projects and teams, helping ensure quality and alignment with global standards.

Global market onboarding: We will expand the Data Engineering Agent deployment across key Vodafone markets including the Czech Republic (CZ), Romania (RO), Ireland (IE), Germany (DE), and the United Kingdom (UK), to drive widespread adoption and modernization.

Integration with developer environments (IDEs): Deepening the integration of agentic capabilities directly into developer workflows (such as VS Code, and and Antigravity) will enable engineers to leverage Data Engineering Agent features within their existing tools and IDEs.

Federated CI/CD governance: Implementing a centralized yet flexible governance framework for Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) will allow individual markets to maintain autonomy while adhering to corporate quality and security policies.

Modernization of legacy stored procedures at scale: By systematically migrating complex, legacy workloads — specifically SAS code, BTEQ scripts, and MicroStrategy — into modern Dataform pipelines will allow us to reduce technical debt and accelerate transformation across the enterprise.

Recent findings suggest that to learn more about transforming your enterprise data architecture for the agentic era, download our complete Data Agents Guidebook or explore Google Cloud’s Rapid Migration and Modernization Program (RaMP). To get started building and optimizing your own data pipelines with the agent today, visit the Data Engineering Agent pipelines documentation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can now assess a seller's security, buy, and deploy supported products in one conversation with AWS Marketplace agent mode, the conversational AI experience for procuring cloud solutions. You share your requirement once, and agent mode applies them as it guides you through discovery, purchase, and deployment.

According to recent reports, describe your use case in natural language to get recommended software, services, AI agents and tools, and multi-product solutions that fit your business needs. To assess a seller's security, request documents such as System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 reports, and get a criterion-by-criterion assessment against a standard cloud security questionnaire, the Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire (CAIQ).

When you're ready to buy, sign in with your AWS account. Agent mode explains pricing and terms so you know what you're committing to, highlights your organizations' purchase requirements, and completes the purchase after you review the terms and confirm. For supported products, agent mode reviews your AWS environment, proposes a deployment proposal with the estimated monthly cost, and deploys after you approve. It then shows you how to start using the product and helps you troubleshoot if a step fails.

Agent mode is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace is available.

To get started, open agent mode on the AWS Marketplace website. To learn more, see Agent mode for AWS Marketplace in the AWS Marketplace Buyer Guide.

ReActWAM: Action-Consistent Caching for Efficient World-Action Models

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (179 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27372v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.

Latest Update: Async GRPO with LoRA across HF Jobs: a bucket, a proxy, and no NCCL

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LoRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14.
  • LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret.
  • According to recent reports, there is also a systems consequence of LoRA training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LoRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14. The asynchronous trainer can now train an adapter instead of the full model, and it syncs only the LoRA adapter to vLLM. This post covers a real-world project built on top of it, where training and inference no longer share a machine.

LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

According to recent reports, there is also a systems consequence of LoRA training. A rank-1 adapter for a 1.5B model is a few megabytes, while the full model is around 3 GB. Instead of sending the full policy to the inference workers after every revision, we can just send the adapter. vLLM can also keep several adapters loaded at once. Old rollouts finish with the policy they started with, while upcoming rollouts use the latest one.

Industry observers note that TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer already separates training and generation. The trainer and vLLM can run on different machines and at their own speed. This is easy in a single-node or cluster setting where both processes share a filesystem or can form an NCCL group.

In a recent development, what we want is to run the same setup with Hugging Face Jobs. Essentially, an HF Job is one container running on one VM. This means that one Job cannot spawn multiple nodes (at least for now) to hold a trainer and a fleet of vLLM servers (we are limited to 8xH200 at most per node). The AsyncGRPOTrainer is built for exactly that kind of scale, so the question became: how far can we get if we drop the requirement that the trainer and the inference servers share a node?

Well, with a full-weight sync, the answer would be "not far". Every enhancement would have to move gigabytes between machines, which is what NCCL is for in a dense cluster, but Jobs can't communicate across nodes. There is no shared local disk and obviously no shared localhost. With LoRA, a sync is only a few megabytes. For the filesystem part, HF Jobs provide volumes backed by Storage Buckets! These buckets can then be mounted as a FUSE filesystem in every Job and are enough to work as a shared FS between nodes. No network path between the Jobs is needed at all.

The setup ended up being quite small:.

The new adapter-only sync path in AsyncGRPOTrainer works like this. The trainer does not send tensors to vLLM. Every few optimizer steps, it saves the adapter under /.vllm_lora/trl-policy-v{N}, publishes the directory with an atomic rename, then sends its path to vLLM's /v1/load_lora_adapter endpoint. vLLM loads the files from disk, so the rollout worker can then request model="trl-policy-v{N}".

Sources indicate that this is how runtime adapter loading already works in vLLM. The endpoint takes a path, not tensors, so the trainer and the server are expected to share a filesystem. On a Slurm cluster, that is the network filesystem. On Jobs, we get the same thing by mounting a Storage Bucket as a volume at the same path in every Job, as we mentioned earlier. Under the hood, it uses hf-mount, which exposes the bucket as a POSIX filesystem inside the container:.

In a recent development, nothing in TRL or vLLM had to change for this. The trainer writes to /lora//.vllm_lora/ and the servers read from the same path. The path sent in the POST request is already valid inside every container.

According to recent reports, note that we also store the checkpoints and the final adapter in the bucket. The HF Jobs are ephemeral, but a preempted trainer can resume training, as the final adapter is always persisted to the bucket and is never lost when the Job stops.

Each replica uses one GPU and the stock vllm/vllm-openai image. We only need to enable runtime LoRA loading and reserve enough adapter slots.

The number of adapter slots follows from max_staleness. In AsyncGRPOTrainer, every weight sync bumps the policy version by one, and max_staleness is how many versions a rollout sample may lag behind the current policy before the trainer discards it. With max_staleness=4, a sample generated under trl-policy-v3 is still used for training while the trainer is at v7. A rollout that started under v3 must also be able to finish under v3. So at any moment, vLLM has to serve the current policy plus the four before it. That is why the trainer keeps max_staleness + 1 adapter versions registered and unloads anything older. Each sync loads the latest version before it unloads the oldest one, which needs one more slot during the swap. That gives --max-loras 6. With only five, vLLM would silently evict a policy that still has rollouts in flight at every sync.

Sources indicate that we pin vLLM to v0.27.1. vLLM moves fast, and the flags above and the runtime LoRA endpoints are the ones that version exposes, so treat the version as part of the recipe.

There is another possible design where the trainer keeps only the latest adapter and always publishes it under the same name. We did not go that way, because vLLM keys its prefix cache by adapter name. With a single name, KV blocks computed under the previous weights would still match after the swap, so the prefill would not be redone and a rollout could get its prefix from one policy version and its decode from the next. The trainer would have no way to tell, and it would show up as ratio drifting away from 1. Versioned names make this impossible: a name always means one set of weights, and a cached prefix can never match a newer version.

We chose sail/Sanity-Test-R1D-1.5B, the dataset from Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16 (Qi et al., 2025). The reproduction code is in sail-sg/Precision-RL.

The authors generated 40 answers for each MATH problem with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. They kept problems with a success rate between 20% and 80%, yielding 1,460 questions. This dataset is really good for RL validation because the questions are neither already solved nor completely hopeless for that model, meaning the model can get a good early signal to train on and improve.

This is awesome as a robust end-to-end test: if one vLLM replica silently serves the base model under an adapter name, we want to see that in the curve within a few dozen steps. Also, this dataset is small enough to cycle through in less than two hours.

We also take the hyperparameters from the paper's LoRA scripts in oat/scripts/lora: Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA rank 1 with alpha 2, a learning rate of 4e-5, 8 samples per prompt, 128 completions per step, a maximum of 3,000 generated tokens and a 4,096-token context.

It has been revealed that the trainer uses the same vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1 image with TRL installed on top. We ran the PR branch at the time; the same code now ships in TRL v1.14. The training script is a normal AsyncGRPOTrainer script. The only Job-specific values are the output directory and the server URL.

During initialization, TRL calls /server_info. If it finds a lora_config, it uses adapter-only sync. Configurations vLLM cannot serve directly, such as DoRA, modules_to_save, or a rank above --max-lora-rank, fall back to merged-weight sync with a warning. The log should contain Adapter-only vLLM sync enabled.

Now onto the fun stuff. We need a proxy between the trainer and the vLLM Jobs for two reasons:.

In a recent development, exposed Job ports require an Authorization: Bearer header on every request. The proxy is where that header gets added, so TRL does not need to know about it.

According to recent reports, we want more than one GPU generating. On a single vLLM server, the usual way to get that is --data-parallel-size > 1, but TRL refuses adapter-only sync in that mode, for a good reason: a call to /v1/load_lora_adapter only reaches the DP rank that answers it, so the other ranks would keep serving the base model under the upcoming policy name. On Jobs the question does not even arise, since each replica is its own machine. So the data parallelism has to live one level up, in something that fans the adapter load out to every replica.

We therefore run a small proxy at 127.0.0.1:8000 on the trainer Job and point TRL to it as if it were a single vLLM server. Besides adding the header, the proxy does two things functionally:.

According to recent reports, A quick reminder of why this matters. Generating a completion has two phases with very different workload profiles:.

In a recent development, those keys and values are the KV cache. Because attention is causal, the KV of a token depends only on the tokens before it, not on what comes after. Two requests that share a prefix therefore share the KV of that prefix, and a replica that already has it in cache can skip that part of the prefill entirely. The whole game now is to find that replica, so a request can benefit from landing on the replica that has already seen its prefix.

Industry observers note that vLLM stores its prefix KV cache in blocks of 16 tokens. Because of GRPO, the rollout worker sends G requests with the same prompt (in our case G=8). If they all reach the same replica, the first request computes the prefill and the next seven reuse it. With round-robin routing, half would go to a replica that doesn't have the prefix cached, and those four requests would redo the prefill work and waste valuable GPU compute.

According to recent reports, the job of our router is to track which replica has seen which block hash. One important detail is that the hashes are chained, so the hash of block 3 represents blocks 1, 2 and 3, not just block 3. This mirrors causal attention: the KV of block 3 is only valid if blocks 1 and 2 are the same too. We also seed the chain with the adapter name because the KV cache also depends on the adapter that generated it: a prefix cached for policy v3 is useless for policy v4!

Sources indicate that the video walks through the entire decision process for choosing a replica. The steps below go through a real 135-token completion request example (from the Sanity dataset problems):.

1. Split the prompt into blocks. The router receives token ids and cuts them into 16-token blocks, just like vLLM. It only hashes complete blocks, so the last 7 tokens are ignored here.

2. Hash the prefix. Each block is hashed with the previous hash, starting from the adapter seed. h3 therefore identifies blocks 1, 2 and 3 in order. Two prompts with the same first k blocks get the same hashes up to hk. Once one block changes, every hash after it changes too. This is why we seed the hashes with the adapter name: the same prompt under trl-policy-v4 starts from another seed and cannot match entries from v3. This is what we want because the old KV blocks were computed with different weights.

Industry observers note that 3. Compare two prompts. Problem 1 has 103 tokens. Both prompts start with the same 23-token chat template. Their first block is identical, but block 2 already contains the problem text. The hashes differ from there.

4. Store the owners. For every hash, the router remembers which replicas served it and which hashes came after it (we cap the successor set at two because we only need to know whether a block has one continuation or several). After a few prompts, the template block h1 is owned by both replicas and already has several successors, h2 to h8 are owned by A only and each has a single successor, and h2' to h6' are owned by B only.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, every prompt in a run starts with the same tokens. Here, it is the chat template and the system prompt, which amount to the first 23 tokens of all 1,460 problems. In an agent setting, it would be the tool descriptions, and in a multi-turn environment it would be the shared conversation history. These blocks are in every replica's cache within seconds, so matching on them tells us nothing about where a particular prompt lives.

Industry observers note that A block is common if every replica has served it, or if it has more than one successor. Common blocks are ignored during routing because they do not identify a particular prompt. More on this below!

Recent findings suggest that 5. Pick a replica. The router counts how many leading blocks match on each replica and removes the common prefix. What is left is the number of blocks specific to this prompt. Then:.

Recent findings suggest that here is the rule applied to four requests. Start from a state where replicas A and B both have 3 requests in flight, and only the template block h1 is known on both replicas.

According to recent reports, 6. Reuse the prefill. Request 2 is the reason for doing all this. It reuses the prefill computed by Request 1: blocks 1 to 8 are already in A's KV cache, so A skips straight to decoding the completion. Had it gone to B, B would have prefilled all 135 tokens again while A's cache sat unused. Request 3 indicates why the common rule is needed. Without it, the shared chat template would make every fresh prompt look like a cache hit. Request 4 keeps the load bounded. Saving one prefill is not worth letting a replica fall far behind.

The common prefix is the annoying part. Every request starts with the same system prompt and chat template. A simple longest-prefix match would give the first replica a match for almost every new prompt. We detect the shared prefix through fan-out instead: a block with several different successors is common, while a block that always leads to the same successor belongs to a particular prompt. Only the blocks after that common prefix count as affinity.

The proxy also needs to broadcast the adapter loads to every replica. We treat the operation as all-or-nothing. Each replica has its own bucket mount, so they do not necessarily see a new adapter at exactly the same time. A No adapter found for error usually means that one bucket mount has not caught up yet, and we retry only that replica. For any other error, we unload the adapter from the replicas that accepted it so that a policy name never exists on only part of the replicas.

We also broadcast /pause, /resume and /v1/unload_lora_adapter in the same way. /health returns 200 only if every replica is healthy. /server_info and /v1/models only need one answer. From TRL's point of view, the proxy is a single data_parallel_size=1 server, so it selects adapter-only sync.

We initially wondered whether a Python asyncio proxy would become a bottleneck. It does not (at least at this scale). There are at most 128 non-streaming JSON requests in flight, and routing only computes a few hashes. One thread handles this easily. A more refined router that needs to handle more traffic would probably need to be written in a faster language (We see you 🦀).

It has been revealed that the numbers below come from the trainer's logged metrics on trackio. The run uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA r=1 on all-linear, 128 completions per step and 8 rollouts per prompt. It runs for 500 steps and saves a checkpoint every 50 steps. The trainer uses an h200x2 Job and each of the two vLLM replicas uses one h200 Job. Running all three costs ~$20 per hour.

Recent findings suggest that all 252 adapter loads succeeded 🎉: 126 syncs times 2 replicas. Six succeeded on the second attempt and 246 on the third.

At the end of the run, after 64,728 rollouts, the proxy's counters read:.

Industry observers note that with 8 rollouts per prompt, at least one of the eight requests must be cold. The theoretical minimum is therefore 12.5 %. The router gets 14.2 % unmatched requests, 84.5 % affinity hits, and 1.3 % spills. There is not much left to gain here unless we start looking at each replica's load using deeper inference-side metrics based on real measured load.

According to recent reports, the first configuration has a pretty obvious problem: the trainer is the bottleneck, not generation. Over the 500 steps, we have:.

The rollout queue stays full, and the worker is mostly blocked by backpressure. The second replica is basically useless in this configuration. We'll see later in the post how we went through runs that moved the bottleneck between training and generation to make the run 3.9× faster.

Figure 1. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: reward with its 20-step rolling mean and 50-step block means, and ratio on a 0.99 to 1.01 axis. Reward climbs from 0.15 to 0.44 over 500 steps; ratio stays between 0.9993 and 1.0004 throughout.

Recent findings suggest that 500 steps took 3 h 27 min. Mean reward goes from 0.145 over the first 20 steps to 0.438 over the last 20. More importantly for this test, ratio stays at 1.000 for every step! The policy served by vLLM always matches the one used by the trainer to score the rollout. This held across all 126 syncs. Mean staleness was 1.5 policy versions, against a maximum of 4. The trackio dashboard has the full curves.

We have our undeniable proof that LoRA AsyncGRPO works! Let's now see how we can improve our training runs by looking at the recent detailed AsyncGRPO metrics.

Async RL is a pipeline between training and generation. Making one side faster does nothing if the other side cannot keep up. Fortunately, in AsyncGRPOTrainer we've added enough timings and metrics to see this directly.

In a recent development, all the useful metrics are documented in the Logged metrics section. perf/rollout_wait_s tells us how long the trainer waits for samples. rollout/backpressure_s tells us how long generation waits for space in the rollout queue. They are diametrically opposed to each other and should not both be high. Together with the queue size, they tell us which side is slow.

We ran five experiments. Each one starts from a problem visible in the previous run's dashboard. Unless mentioned otherwise, the model, recipe and three-Job layout stay the same. The names below are the trackio run names.

We keep these four groups of metrics visible:.

Sources indicate that the diagnosis is simple: a full queue with zero rollout wait and high backpressure means the trainer is too slow. An empty queue with rising rollout wait and no backpressure means generation is too slow. Comparing perf/mfu_wall_clock with perf/mfu_fwd_bwd also indicates how much time the trainer GPUs spend waiting instead of training.

In a recent development, figure 2. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, rollout/backpressure_s. Step time and forward+backward overlap almost completely; the queue sits pinned near 476 of 512 and backpressure never drops below 11 s per rollout group: trainer-bound.

It has been revealed that perf/step_s is 22.9 s and perf/fwd_bwd_s is 21.9 s. Forward and backward take 96 % of the step time. The queue stays full and the trainer waits only 0.02 s for rollouts, and the rollout worker spends 15 seconds per group blocked by backpressure. The two vLLM replicas generate faster than the trainer consumes. The reported 4.6k tokens/s is not their actual limit; they simply have nowhere to put more output.

In a recent development, the batch metrics explain the terrible 3.9 % MFU. batch/microbatches_per_step is 64 and batch/samples_per_row is 1.0. Each rank processes one sequence of around 1.2k tokens, 64 times per step. This comes from the reference recipe's per_device_train_batch_size=1. For a 1.5B model on an H200, this is completely latency-bound.

Recent findings suggest that the fix is not to change the batch size. We keep 128 completions per optimizer step and only change how they are laid out on the GPU: instead of one sequence per microbatch, we pack many sequences densely into each row. The trainer supports this through token-budget batching. With token_budget > 0, it packs several samples into one padding-free row per rank. An optimizer step processes gradient_accumulation_steps rows. We set token_budget=16384 and gradient_accumulation_steps=6.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp2-tb16k overlaid over their first 154 steps. Panels: batch/samples_per_row, batch/microbatches_per_step, perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd, rollout/generated_tok_s. Packing takes samples per row from 1 to 13, microbatches from 64 to 6, step time from 23 s to 5.9 s, and generation from 4.2k to 27.5k tok/s with no change on the vLLM side.

Industry observers note that batch/samples_per_row goes from 1.0 to ~12.7 and the number of microbatches drops from 64 to 6. The rows are 95 % full! Forward and backward fall from 21.9 s to 5.6 s, while MFU rises from 3.9 % to 19 %. We now train on around 150 samples per step because the rows pack better than the mean-length estimate predicted.

Generation also jumps from 4.6k to 25k tokens/s, even though we changed nothing on the vLLM side. The queue is no longer constantly full, so the replicas can finally run. This is why we do not like optimizing pipeline stages in isolation. We need to be careful to evaluate the whole system, as a slow stage can hide the real performance of everything before it.

It has been revealed that perf/fwd_s is 1.34 s while perf/fwd_bwd_s is 5.6 s. A normal backward costs roughly twice the forward, and with frozen base weights it should be closer to once. A ratio of 3.2 is suspicious.

The reason is that AsyncGRPOConfig defaults to gradient_checkpointing=True. Every microbatch recomputes its forward during the backward. This also explains why a 16k-token row only uses 25 GB on a 141 GB H200! It's a memory optimization for this trainer, but we don't need it in this specific case: the model is small enough to fit into VRAM with the activations kept for the backward.

It has been revealed that figure 4. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k and r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/fwd_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/weight_sync_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, perf/rollout_wait_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd. Forward+backward drops by one forward; the queue falls from ~420 to ~60, and rollout wait rises from 0.02 s to 0.5 s: the bottleneck shifts to generation.

With gradient_checkpointing=False, forward and backward drop to 4.6 s, almost exactly one forward less, and MFU reaches 23 %. The queue now falls to 71 and rollout wait rises from 0.04 s to 0.6 s. The trainer consumes samples faster than two replicas generate them. We successfully moved the bottleneck to generation.

In a recent development, this exposes two more costs. A 7.6-second weight sync every four steps now takes 25 % of wall-clock time. It was only 8 % when each step took 23 seconds. Also, backward is still 2.5 times slower than forward. With frozen base weights, there are around 2 seconds per step that do not look like normal model math.

Since generation was now too slow, we added a third replica. We also reduced the adapter retry interval from 2 s to 0.5 s in the proxy and disabled fsdp_reshard_after_forward to check whether FSDP2 re-gathers caused the extra 2 seconds in backward.

Figure 5. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt and r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/weight_sync_s, rollout/generated_tok_s, rollout/inflight, perf/fwd_bwd_s. Sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s; generation and forward+backward do not move; rollout/inflight reads 128 in both runs, which is the cap the third replica ran into.

Weight sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s, so the shorter retry helps. Forward and backward stay at 4.6 s, which rules out resharding. Generation moves from 25k to only 26k tokens/s. The third replica does basically nothing.

In a recent development, the reason was sitting in rollout/inflight: 128 in every run. The proxy shows those requests split as 44 + 43 + 41 across the three replicas. max_inflight_tasks limits concurrency for the whole rollout worker, not per replica. A 1.5B model on an H200 processes 43 and 130 concurrent sequences at almost the same cost per token. Splitting 128 requests over three GPUs gives nearly the same throughput as splitting them over two.

So vLLM was not the limit. Our own client-side constant was. We had set it conservatively because we did not know how hundreds of long HTTPS requests would behave through the public Jobs proxy. At this point, 130,000 rollout completions had crossed it without a single transport error.

max_inflight_tasks=384 and queue_maxsize=768, nothing else.

Industry observers note that figure 6. All five trackio runs (r1-dp2, r1-dp2-tb16k, r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-inflight384) overlaid, x-axis in steps. Panels: perf/step_s, reward, sample/rollout_queue_size, sample/staleness_mean. Step time falls from 22.9 s to 4.8 s across the series while the reward curves stay on top of each other; the last run's queue refills to ~690 of 768 and its staleness settles at 2. Runs 2 to 4 were stopped early once the dashboard had answered the question.

Industry observers note that with 384 requests in flight, each replica gets 128. The queue rapidly fills to around 690 out of 768 and stays there. Backpressure returns to 5 seconds and rollout wait falls to 0.03 seconds. Training is the bottleneck again! Forward and backward take 4.6 seconds, weight sync adds an amortized 1.5 seconds, and median step time is 4.8 seconds.

It has been revealed that mean staleness rises from 1.5 to 2.0 versions because samples wait longer in the larger queue. This is still below max_staleness=4, and ratio remains very close to 1.000.

Industry observers note that figure 7. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp3-inflight384, reward against wall-clock minutes since the first optimizer step. Same recipe, same 500 steps, same final reward; run 5 gets there in 52 minutes instead of 3 h 26 min.

The final run is 3.9× faster and trains on 31 % more samples, with basically the same reward curve. Packing, disabling checkpointing and raising the in-flight limit made the difference. In each case, the dashboard made this clear within the first ten minutes.

According to recent reports, loRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with sportzfy rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

Really interesting take on how LoRA changes the systems side of RL training, not just the training itself. The idea of separating training and inference across different machines while only moving a small adapter instead of the full model makes a lot of practical sense, especially when working with HF Jobs. The “bucket, proxy, and no NCCL” approach feels like a good example of simplifying distributed infrastructure by moving the communication boundary to something much smaller and easier to manage.

I also like the connection to the LoRA Without Regret work, particularly the point that policy-gradient updates may not require huge adapter capacity to capture the useful signal. Sending only a few MB instead of several GB after updates can make a massive difference in both bandwidth and iteration speed. Would be really interested to see more details on how the bucket/proxy setup behaves at scale and whether there are any noticeable trade-offs once the number of inference workers or concurrent rollouts increases.

AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (199 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27369v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged checkpoint that concentrates transfer in high-utility, low-interference directions. We evaluate AMARIS on Qwen3-based merges (8B and 32B) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA specialization. In our evaluated settings, AMARIS reaches Pareto operating points that are competitive with strong training-free baselines, including 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention for the 8B finance setting, 103.55% core retention with 90.28% specialist retention for the 8B instruction-following setting, and 99.20% core retention with 94.80% specialist retention for the 32B SEA setting. These results support subspace-constrained merging as a practical route to compositional capability integration without additional training.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Lambda unveils OpenTelemetry (OTel) support for Lambda durable functions. You can now trace your durable executions and emit traces to Amazon CloudWatch and other industry-standard observability tools. This helps you find bottlenecks in your system, root cause failures faster, and understand how your workflows behave in production.

In a recent development, with Lambda durable functions, you can build resilient, multi-step applications and AI workflows that run for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing and automatic retries. Durable functions can run for hours, or days, suspending and resuming across many Lambda invocations. The fresh OpenTelemetry plugin emits a unified trace that spans a full durable execution, including steps, waits, callbacks, and chained function invocations. You can use the trace to gain operational insights across your executions including step durations, retries, and failures across executions.

The OpenTelemetry plugin is available for the TypeScript, Python, and Java SDKs. You can enable OpenTelemetry support by adding the OpenTelemetry plugin package alongside the Durable Execution SDK and register it on your durable handler or using an environment variable. OpenTelemetry support for Lambda durable functions is available in all AWS Regions that support Lambda durable functions.

To get started, see the  OpenTelemetry plugin documentation, the plugin interface documentation, and the sample application. To learn more, read the blog post.

Director, Engineering, Google Ads.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Ever wonder how the Google Ads team keeps the massive system stable and online, despite continuous attempts by hackers to take it down? Part of the answer is using Spanner as its core operational and graph database.

Sources indicate that the Google Ads team uses a central graph-based platform to fight fraud and abuse with batch and real-time signals. Built to protect the Google Ads ecosystem and now used by multiple teams across Google, the platform organizes anti-abuse intelligence into a single, interconnected view. Its core mission is simple but critical: uncover hidden connections between malicious assets in real time before they can harm owners or advertisers. This blog talks about the challenging modern fraud and abuse landscape, and how Spanner, specifically Spanner Graph, helps Google successfully detect those threats.

The need for a graph-based abuse detection platform stems from how the global threat landscape has evolved. Digital advertising fraud and online scams are no longer minor operational nuisances, they are a massive drain on the global economy. According to the NASDAQ Global Financial Crime Report, total global fraud losses are estimated at nearly $580 billion for 2025. Furthermore, global surveys indicate that approximately one in five adults fall victim to scams. In digital ads, fraud and abuse waste marketing spend, corrupt attribution data, and expose everyday users to financial scams, identity theft, and malware.

Bad actors are increasingly leveraging automation and AI to scale deceptive campaigns more efficiently. In 2025 alone, Google blocked or removed more than 8.3 billion policy-violating ads and suspended 24.9 million advertiser accounts. As these tactics evolve, real-time detection becomes more vital for protecting businesses and users.

Defending applications from fraud and abuse requires continuously advancing threat detection beyond traditional, point-in-time checks. To do that, modern security systems must address two compounding challenges simultaneously:.

Fraud and abuse operate as networks: Bad actors hide behind residential proxies and synthetic identities to create deceptive ad campaigns. Each of the attributes like location proxies, account, and identity parameters  appear benign in isolation. But behind the scenes, bad actors share payment methods, domains, and accounts, requiring security systems to target entire coordinated clusters of fraud rather than isolated indicators. This is hard to capture with traditional approaches that do not understand the relationship between attributes and evaluates each signal separately.

According to recent reports, detection must scale dynamically: As the graph-based abuse detection platform grew, the previous system, based on offline MapReduce batch processing, became bottlenecked. Tracing multi-hop relationships in batch MapReduce required repeated, expensive joins across distributed stages, triggering massive intermediate data expansions, heavy shuffle overhead, and network bottlenecks that caused hours-long latencies and combinatorial fanouts during multi-hop traversals.

According to recent reports, in critical scenarios like halting live malware campaigns, multi-hour latency gaps leave room for a lot of damage. To block sophisticated fraud rings, Google needed to evaluate multi-hop relationship risks in real time at the time of serving these ads, before malicious content reaches customers.

To overcome the limits of processing at inference time, the engineering team needed a database that could ingest live signals from a large number of sources via pub/sub streams, all while delivering horizontal elasticity, global transactional consistency, and sub-second multi-hop traversals. The solution was to modernize Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for Ads onto Spanner Graph.

In a recent development, because Ads’ core transactional and entity data already lived in Spanner, they didn’t need to migrate any data in order to adopt Spanner Graph. Rather than standing up a separate, specialized graph database, the team simply defined property graphs directly on top of their existing relational tables.

This delivered several benefits:.

From hour-long batch jobs to sub-second queries: Spanner Graph co-locates graph traversal computations directly with the underlying distributed data splits to minimize join overhead. Multi-hop traversals that previously took an hour in offline Apache Flume MapReduce jobs now execute on live production data with sub-second to single-digit millisecond latency.

According to recent reports, zero-ETL adoption in weeks, not months: Because there was no data to move, most graph-based abuse detection use cases transitioned to Spanner Graph within weeks. Layering a graph directly onto existing Spanner tables eliminated fragile synchronization pipelines and redundant storage costs.

Expressive pattern matching with native ISO GQL: Instead of writing and maintaining complex custom traversal code, engineers now query the exact same tables using standard ISO Graph Query Language (GQL), significantly accelerating feature velocity.

Sources indicate that with Spanner Graph, Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for ads performs multi-hop pattern matching directly against operational relational data using ISO GQL. For instance, when an account is flagged for suspicious activity, the platform does real-time traversals to uncover all connected signals across the graph. This allows security systems to identify and disable entire coordinated fraud rings rapidly rather than handling individual accounts sequentially.

Today, the graph-based abuse detection platform operates as a unified, Google-wide defense platform across a live graph of over 500 billion nodes and 1 trillion edges. Further, bringing ability to do multi-hop graph queries to real-time enforcement has fundamentally changed how Google stops abuse, delivering big wins for customers and end people:.

Safeguarding advertiser budgets: The graph-based abuse detection platform is a primary source of detection signals for ad policy enforcement across Google's ad products. By uncovering the coordinated networks behind click fraud, click farms, and invalid traffic in real time, it stops bad actors, so advertisers don’t waste budget on invalid interactions.

Defending users against emerging threats: Real-time relationship analysis helps Google catch public-figure impersonation, account takeovers, cloaking, and landing-page malware before campaigns start to scale. During any incident, the graph-based abuse detection platform plays a vital role in tracing the connected assets and rapidly shutting down the attack.

Stopping repeat financial offenders: By correlating billing, financial, and identity information the platform identifies repeat bad actors and prevents banned offenders from simply spinning up latest accounts to evade enforcement.

Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for ads shows what Spanner Graph can deliver under the world’s most demanding scale and latency requirements. Because this unified relational and graph architecture is built directly into Spanner, enterprises across a variety of industries can use the same foundation to solve their own complex pattern-matching and fraud challenges:.

Retail and e-commerce: Retailers connect customer accounts, payments, and shipping data to stop promo abuse and bot networks at checkout. For instance, Target rebuilt its Gift Finder using Spanner Graph and vector search (GraphRAG), cutting maintenance by 50% with sub-10ms latency. Additionally, PayPal uses Spanner Graph for its Customer Graph to unify customer identities across brands.

Sources indicate that cybersecurity and threat intelligence: Security teams map network assets, login origins, and access permissions to uncover attack paths and isolate compromised infrastructure during live incidents. Unifying graph queries with relational telemetry in Spanner helps expose proxy networks and automated impersonators before lateral movement occurs.

Financial services and payments: Risk teams correlate billing data and payment instruments to stop synthetic identity rings and fraud. Equifax uses Spanner Graph to map ownership hierarchies across 30 million businesses.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27365v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to consumers' devices keeps sensitive data local and reduces inference cost, but deploying a specialized model per capability duplicates vision-language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. We formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD), measuring how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. High HCD across representation, generation, and decision raises two challenges: these capabilities need visual evidence at different spatial granularities under a fixed token budget, and separately collected task corpora yield conflicting updates to shared parameters, while cross-task paired supervision is costly and ambiguous for open-ended inputs. We present WePM, a family of pocket models unifying representation, generation, and decision within one vision-language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks; Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding cross-task paired annotation; Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task's contribution through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, with sequential gradient accumulation under memory constraints. In the joint representation-generation setting, WePM outperforms all baselines across five evaluation groups, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluation, WePM-4B attains the best average score over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks (72.86, 62.41, 61.11). Against the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.
