#24210. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1822 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.
  • In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request.
  • Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

That is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

In an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a new guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

In a recent development, standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Recent findings suggest that mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

Sources indicate that this isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

It has been revealed that the shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

In a recent development, this is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a newly introduced source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

In a recent development, 2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":.

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

It has been revealed that the consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

According to recent reports, the middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

In a recent development, the sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

Industry observers note that if accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an problem or a discussion.

In a recent development, great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”.

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

Sources indicate that what I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

On your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:.

I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each fresh task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

arXiv:2611.27350v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: GraphRAG combines a language model's parametric knowledge with retrieved graph evidence, yet aggregate accuracy cannot show whether failures stem from missing paths, distractors, or conflicts with model knowledge. We introduce GRACE, a benchmark built by executing LC-QuAD 2.0 queries over Wikidata and applying four controlled interventions to each evidence subgraph: severing a support path, adding type-compatible distractors, attaching high-degree hubs, and replacing the supported answer with a counterfactual entity. Questions and option positions remain fixed across the five states. The validated benchmark contains 4,028 questions and 20,140 question-graph pairs. These comparisons reveal that question-only routing cannot distinguish evidence states, while relevance guidance can improve answerable states yet hurt when the support path is severed: relevant facts may not jointly suffice to answer. We propose QCFSE-SA, which combines typed local attention, global graph attention, and question-conditioned evidence guidance with a calibrated graph-support gate. With the factual context and generator held fixed, it improves controlled-state accuracy from 57.17% to 62.78% (+5.61 points; question-clustered 95% CI [+5.04, +6.17]) and broken-state accuracy from 55.41% to 67.85%. According to recent reports, amazon Connect Customer announces the general availability of Resolutions, an agentic operations solution that resolves high-volume work end-to-end, including refund requests, transaction disputes, fraud investigations, and insurance claims. Resolutions helps businesses reduce resolution times and cost to serve by combining the reasoning of AI agents with the reliability of deterministic workflows. Every request follows business policy, gets the oversight it requires, and ends in a verifiable outcome.

Managers describe a process in natural language or upload standard operating procedures (SOPs), and Resolutions generates a Work strategy in minutes. As it builds the Work plan, Resolutions asks clarifying questions that surface exceptions, set decision rules, and define approval thresholds, closing the gaps an SOP leaves open. Resolutions then opens a Resolutions Case for each incoming request and applies the right Work plan. AI agents gather information, apply policy, act across your business applications, and ask customers for missing details to drive every Case to completion. Each Step can run on prebuilt AI agents, AI agents configured in Amazon Connect Customer, or your own, while human specialists handle approvals and exceptions with the context they need to act.

For example, a bank resolving a transaction dispute can have AI agents pull the transaction history, check the claim against chargeback rules, email the cardholder for a missing receipt, and issue a provisional credit, so a specialist reviews only the disputes that need judgment. Resolutions verifies each outcome and records every action and decision, giving operations leaders an auditable, real-time view of progress, workload, and service level risk.

To learn more, visit our documentation, webpage, and pricing page.

#24204. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1567 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

Recent findings suggest that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

Industry observers note that this work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project highlighted they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

It has been revealed that v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

Recent findings suggest that the model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

In a recent development, the tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Sources indicate that each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

Recent findings suggest that that regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Industry observers note that real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

It has been revealed that naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Upcoming words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

Recent findings suggest that the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated newly introduced memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

It has been revealed that v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

Recent findings suggest that the overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

Industry observers note that A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we strategy to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

#24202. Latest Update: EcomWriteBench: A Real-World Benchmark for E-commerce Writing Tasks

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: EcomWriteBench: A Real-World Benchmark for E-commerce Writing Tasks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (200 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27349v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used throughout e-commerce workflows to generate content that informs purchasing decisions and supports customer interactions. Evaluating these systems requires accounting for user needs, product evidence, structural constraints, and business requirements that are not fully captured by general-purpose writing benchmarks. We introduce EcomWriteBench, a real-world benchmark containing 3,861 queries from 69 e-commerce writing tasks across 13 categories and five languages. Through task-level extraction, cross-task consolidation, and refinement guided by human feedback, EcomWriteBench constructs a shared pool of 37 abilities and identifies the subset applicable to each task. Ability-wise scoring enables us to compare state-of-the-art LLMs on EcomWriteBench and characterize their relative strengths and weaknesses across fine-grained e-commerce writing abilities. We further propose a preference-calibrated weight-learning framework that converts human pairwise preferences into interpretable scoring rubrics through global, category-level, and task-level aggregation weights. This framework provides a reusable approach for translating human preferences into automated evaluation by combining ability discovery, ability-wise scoring, and preference-calibrated aggregation, and can potentially be applied to a broad range of benchmarks beyond EcomWriteBench. On held-out queries, our scoring framework achieves 88.96% agreement with human preferences, compared with 78.54% for conventional LLM-as-a-judge scoring.

Industry News: What’s new in Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As organizations move from reactive analytics to proactive systems of action powered by autonomous AI agents, data platforms face a new set of demands.
  • In the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation.
  • Today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

As organizations move from reactive analytics to proactive systems of action powered by autonomous AI agents, data platforms face a new set of demands. Moving from human scale to agent scale changes both how data pipelines run and how they are built: Teams and AI agents now use Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and agentic troubleshooting to build, submit, and diagnose Apache Spark pipelines while preparing multimodal datasets, performing feature engineering, and acting on live business signals around the clock. Over the past year, customer use of Managed Service for Apache Spark in serverless deployments has nearly doubled, with millions of jobs running each month as enterprises build on Google’s Agentic Data Cloud.

In the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation. Managed Service for Apache Spark runs on Google Cloud's borderless lakehouse, so Apache Spark and BigQuery can read and write the same tables with high performance. Through Knowledge Catalog, both engines share centralized governance, consistent policies, detailed lineage, and semantic discovery for AI agents.

Today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments. Engineered to power both modern enterprise data pipelines and fast-growing agentic workloads, Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 introduces:.

A new 4.0 runtime with Apache Spark 4.2: Standardized on Apache Spark 4.2, Java 25, Python 3.13 with Pixi, and Apache Iceberg 1.12, it is now available for both serverless and managed clusters.

A redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console and agentic troubleshooting: Onboard quickly with a upcoming Overview page featuring a samples gallery, Lakehouse public datasets, and one-click VS Code authoring in Cloud Shell, manage all serverless and cluster workloads from a unified Jobs view, and use an AI agent to automatically diagnose job failures.

Third-party IDE integration with the Data Agent Kit: Configure MCP servers, skills, and API access to build and run Apache Spark pipelines directly from VS Code, Claude Code, and Antigravity.

Faster startups and Lightning Engine acceleration: Run on default Gen4 infrastructure with faster startups at no additional cost, and accelerate workloads with Lightning Engine for up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative.

This upcoming runtime packages Apache Spark 4.2 (including Spark Declarative Pipelines and Real-Time Mode), Java 25, Scala 2.13, Apache Iceberg 1.12, Delta Lake 4.4, and Python 3.13 with Pixi for faster dependency management.

Managed Spark serverless and cluster workloads now run on the same modern stack whether written by a data engineer or generated by data engineering and data science skills in Gemini, Claude, and other large language models (LLMs). Teams can standardize on one set of component versions and move PySpark, Scala, and Spark SQL workloads between serverless and managed clusters.

Data teams should spend their time writing Spark logic rather than configuring infrastructure, hunting for the right job, or digging through driver and executor logs when something fails. Version 4.0 ships alongside a redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console built to take that operational work off their plate.

The refreshed console streamlines every stage of the Apache Spark lifecycle:.

Frictionless onboarding and one-click authoring: A redesigned Overview page helps developers get started immediately with an integrated samples gallery, pre-loaded Lakehouse public datasets, guided demos, and one-click authoring in VS Code through Cloud Shell.

Optimized defaults and reusable runtime profiles: Out-of-the-box performance defaults simplify job submission and cluster creation. With reusable runtime profiles (in preview) for batch and interactive workloads, platform admins can capture governed hardware, network, and autoscaling baselines once so developers can simply select a profile and run code.

Unified job, session, and fleet management: Engineers can submit and monitor batch jobs, interactive serverless sessions, and managed clusters from a single unified listing, backed by streamlined fleet management and redesigned detail views that surface key performance metrics and logs in one place.

Agentic troubleshooting: When a job fails or slows down, an AI agent analyzes logs, metrics, and query intends within existing IAM permissions to identify the likely root cause and recommend a fix, helping engineers quickly return a failed job to a healthy state.

Image 1: Gemini Cloud Assist investigates a failed Apache Spark job, forms a hypothesis, and points to the likely root cause without leaving the job page.

Image 2: One Jobs page for every Apache Spark workload across serverless and managed clusters, with tier and runtime version at a glance.

Many data engineers and data scientists would rather never leave their editor. With the Data Agent Kit, they can build and run Apache Spark workloads from VS Code, Antigravity, Claude Code, and other agentic IDEs. Setup takes a few clicks: pick Apache Spark and the other services you use, and the kit configures Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agent skills, and API access for each one. From there, AI agents can generate, tune, and test Apache Spark pipelines on Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 without leaving the IDE.

Image 3: In VS Code, the Data Agent Kit sets up MCP servers, skills, and API access for Apache Spark and other services.

According to recent reports, as practitioners and AI agents trigger short-running, ephemeral jobs on demand to prepare data, perform feature engineering, and answer ad-hoc queries, low startup latency and predictable price-performance are essential to avoiding a cost spiral. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, our performance-optimized serverless experience removes manual infrastructure tuning through three changes:.

Faster startups at no additional cost: On the serverless Premium tier, runtime and control-plane optimizations in version 4.0 deliver faster startup times than previous runtime versions across interactive sessions and short-running batch workloads at no additional cost.

It has been revealed that hardware acceleration by default: Fresh serverless 4.0 workloads run on the Premium tier by default, using Google Cloud's latest-generation Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk storage. Teams get our highest-efficiency compute and storage fleet without picking machine types or configuring disks, while aligning infrastructure tiering directly with workload urgency.

Sources indicate that software acceleration with Lightning Engine: Our native C++ vectorized execution engine, Lightning Engine, is available in the 4.0 runtime and delivers up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative, along with up to 4.9x faster performance compared to running open-source Apache Spark with zero code changes. Built on Apache Gluten and Velox with Google-specific optimizations, Lightning Engine compiles Apache Spark DataFrame, Dataset, and Spark SQL query looks into native SIMD instructions. For lakehouse storage, built-in intelligent caching accelerates file scan times on Apache Iceberg tables by up to 50%. Separately, for workloads querying BigQuery, Lightning Engine's native reader uses Apache Arrow streams to accelerate BigQuery reads by up to 40% compared to default BigQuery reads in Managed Service for Apache Spark. In the 4.0 runtime, Lightning Engine expands support to ARM processors, Ubuntu images, and native vectorized readers for Apache ORC and CSV alongside Apache Parquet, Apache Iceberg, and Delta Lake.

It has been revealed that "We were facing not only processing challenges, we were facing management overhead across thousands of servers in our ecosystem, so we migrated to serverless Managed Service for Apache Spark. We moved from managing infrastructure to a no-ops infrastructure. Not only did it help us overcome maintenance and cluster management challenges, it helped us optimize our costs at scale to meet our business SLAs. Apache Spark is no longer just compute for us; it is a strategic business accelerator."—Saurabh Kumar, Senior Director of Data Engineering, Lowe's.

It has been revealed that when autonomous agents and production pipelines run around the clock, tying a workload to a single machine shape or zone can stall downstream decisions when regional demand spikes. Without dedicated reservations, cloud service providers may not always have available capacity during peak demand. We are introducing infrastructure fungibility for serverless deployments to improve resource availability for all customers:.

Sources indicate that serverless infrastructure fungibility and fallback: Serverless 4.0 workloads are no longer tied to one VM instance family, disk type, or zone. The platform selects from several latest-generation VM instance families and disk types across zones in the region. If the preferred infrastructure is constrained during a local demand peak, the service automatically chooses the best available infrastructure in the same region instead of failing the job. Once capacity returns, workloads go back to the default Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk infrastructure.

In a recent development, data Compute Unit (DCU) quotas: Quotas for serverless deployments are now set in DCUs rather than per machine family. Because the platform selects the VM instance family, admins manage one unified DCU quota instead of separate CPU quotas for each machine type.

A borderless lakehouse breaks down walled gardens by connecting operational, analytical, and cross-cloud data in open formats without moving it. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, Apache Iceberg ships directly in the runtime image, and every workload automatically has access to the serverless Lakehouse runtime catalog. Teams no longer have to configure a lakehouse metastore with Apache Spark or complete prerequisites such as setting up Google Cloud Storage (GCS) directories beforehand, so they can focus straight on writing business logic. Version 4.0 also eliminates the need for GCS staging buckets and uses end-user credentials by default.

It has been revealed that through the Lakehouse runtime catalog, Managed Service for Apache Spark, BigQuery, and AlloyDB can directly read and write the same Apache Iceberg tables on GCS without ETL pipelines or data copies. Everything registered in the Lakehouse runtime catalog automatically surfaces in Knowledge Catalog, which enriches metadata and business context so AI agents and Gemini can query and reason over tables curated with Apache Spark with high accuracy, governed access controls, and lower token costs.

To see how these capabilities come together across end-to-end architectures, read our Google Cloud Apache Spark in the Agentic Era whitepaper. The whitepaper walks through practical design patterns for multimodal data preparation, large-scale feature engineering, and connecting AI agents to governed Apache Iceberg tables through MCP tools and Knowledge Catalog.

Sources indicate that managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 is available for serverless and managed cluster deployments across all Managed Service for Apache Spark regions. The fastest way to try version 4.0 is the Data Agent Kit: install it in VS Code, Claude Code, or Antigravity to build and run Apache Spark workloads on version 4.0 with AI agents right from your IDE. You can also start from the new Overview page in the Google Cloud console, which walks you from code to a running job.

To learn more, read the Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 documentation for serverless deployments and managed clusters, and try the hands-on Lightning Engine codelab.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon CloudFront now lets web development platforms and SaaS providers move a customer's domain to their platform in a single request with no downtime, and serve requests to the domain while the TLS certificate is being configured.
  • Sources indicate that previously, moving a domain that was already in use required disabling the original distribution, using a wildcard workaround, or contacting AWS Support.
  • According to recent reports, these features are available in all edge locations at no additional cost.

Amazon CloudFront now lets web development platforms and SaaS providers move a customer's domain to their platform in a single request with no downtime, and serve requests to the domain while the TLS certificate is being configured. The CloudFront multi-tenant distributions allow these platforms to serve many customer domains from one shared configuration. Together, these features help move existing AWS customers to multi-tenant distributions without impacting their traffic.

Sources indicate that previously, moving a domain that was already in use required disabling the original distribution, using a wildcard workaround, or contacting AWS Support. Now you can bring customer domains onto your multi-tenant setup as part of creating or updating a tenant. With the fresh OnDomainTakeover option, CloudFront checks domain ownership through DNS records and then moves one or more domains in a single request. This works within an AWS account or across accounts. If you add a domain before its certificate is issued, CloudFront serves it over HTTP until you attach a certificate. That gives you time to validate the domain with AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) or another certificate authority and attach the certificate once it's issued.

According to recent reports, these features are available in all edge locations at no additional cost. To learn more, see Move domains and Domains without a certificate in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (220 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.27330v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: A planner deciding whether to turn left or continue straight needs to inspect different parts of the scene for each maneuver. Yet many end-to-end driving planners evaluate every candidate trajectory against the same compressed scene representation. We let each candidate select the visual evidence used to refine and score it. A global glance first produces trajectory hypotheses from shared scene features. We then project a corridor around each trajectory into the camera views and use the resulting mask to attend to patch features at the backbone's native resolution. After refinement, the scorer projects each final proposal again and ranks it using evidence along its own path. This geometric selection requires only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration. On three planners with different scene representations (learned registers, a perception-supervised bird's-eye-view grid, and a coarse image-token grid), adding this gaze improves planning scores. In ablations, path-aligned patches outperform both a matched number of randomly selected patches and attention over all patches. Using the gaze for ranking yields larger gains than using it for refinement alone. With a ViT-S backbone and no perception labels, GGDriver achieves a rater feedback score of 8.110 on the WOD-E2E test set, 94.2 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1, 48.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM-v2, and a closed-loop Driving Score of 72.18 on Bench2Drive.

#24196. How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3149 w)

How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance challenges.
  • By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff.
  • Sources indicate that the staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance challenges.

By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff.

Sources indicate that the staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.

In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.

Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains.

Software work evolves from manual labor to partnering with machines to agent factories.

It has been revealed that 1. Pre-Codex. Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools.

2. Codex as a partner. Once we had Codex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

According to recent reports, 3. Reusable skills. To automate further, we captured our performance team’s investigation process in a shared skill called perf-forensics. It tells Codex which tools are available, when to use them, and how to work through a slowdown so Codex can try to resolve the problem from a few angles:.

Investigate whether deployments or configuration changes could explain it.

We tested and refined the perf-forensics skill using evals based on past regressions. For the types of regressions we focused on (for example, ChatGPT latency and availability drops), we could now give Codex an alert and get back a diagnosis in a single run, without guiding it through each step.

It has been revealed that 4. The human proxy. As we added and refined perf-related Codex skills like perf-forensics, we started to feel like a proxy between our alerts and Codex. An alert would fire, and an engineer would simply copy and paste it into Codex with the right skill, then paste the findings back into Slack.

5. Automated investigations. Next, we moved investigations to the cloud so an alert could start a Codex session automatically. Codex investigated the slowdown and posted its findings in the Slack thread, but the automation ended with that reply. An engineer still had to pick up the diagnosis, develop a fix, and check whether it worked after deployment. As alerts accumulated, even figuring out which regressions needed attention meant sifting through Slack threads.

6. The factory. We built the Performance Factory to run end-to-end agentic performance engineering workflows. It tracks what each active task needs next and assigns an agent when that step is ready. Each task keeps its state and findings, so work can pass between agents and engineers and resume after a code review or deployment. For a regression, the work starts with investigating an alert and ends with verifying recovery in production. We can turn common optimizations into workflows that run regularly across our services. A workflow that spots a potential optimization can open a task in another workflow to test and implement it.

The Performance Factory is made up of four components: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a dispatch loop that assigns ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes (such as a GitHub review comment posting or a deployment completing).

Performance Factory consists of a task service, dispatch loop, cloud execution, and subscriptions.

Recent findings suggest that the task service is where engineers define workflows by adding configuration files and prompts for the agents to follow, written in Markdown. The configuration lists the states a task can move through, the allowed transitions, and which steps need an engineer. Separate prompts tell agents what to do at each step.

A code change task contains a configuration file, along with Markdown prompts for implementing and reviewing.

According to recent reports, each piece of work becomes a task in a workflow, and all workflows are visible in a UI. Engineers can see what’s open, follow progress, and share a task with a teammate who might have more context or be able to help with the next step.

A dispatch loop periodically checks which tasks are ready for the next step. It assigns an agent to each task by starting a Codex turn with the instructions for the task’s current state. The agent records its progress on the task and moves it to the next state if it completes the step.

Sources indicate that once a task is assigned, the agent needs a place to do the work, with access to the same tools an engineer would use. We built an internal API to programmatically invoke a Codex turn in the cloud. The Codex turn runs on an environment inside our network, with access to our code repositories and the observability tools our engineers use, such as metrics, logs, traces, CPU profiles, and memory snapshots.

In a recent development, the agent runs under a service identity, so we can scope its permissions and see which actions came from our performance agents. Moving agentic work to the cloud lets us run work in parallel without relying on engineers’ laptops being open or manually managing individual cloud development boxes.

Finding, root causing, and solving regressions is the first workflow we built inside the Performance Factory. We call it the Regression Workflow. A performance regression moves through several stages: needs investigation, root caused, fix proposed, and resolved, so we built the automated workflow to reflect and move a task through those same stages.

When one of its configured performance alerts fires, the Regression Workflow opens a task that agents pick up and move across these stages. The task records its status and key findings outside of any one agent’s context so that other agents or engineers can pick up the work. Engineers can follow the work in Slack or the Regression Workflow UI, add context, and review proposed changes. After a fix is deployed, an agent checks whether the performance has recovered to its original state before resolving the task.

The Regression Workflow’s steps include finding the root cause, proposing a fix, reviewing and deploying, and verifying recovery.

Recent findings suggest that finding the root cause (or causes) is the first major step in the workflow. The agent starts by figuring out which metrics got worse, when they started to change, and which service requests were affected. The perf-forensics skill gives Codex access to the tools our performance engineers use and a playbook for working through those questions.

An alert fires when a metric crosses a threshold, but the regression may have started hours earlier. The agent looks back through the data to find when the metric first got worse. It then compares groups of requests: did similar requests actually get slower, or were we serving more requests that were already slow? Those findings point to different causes.

Sources indicate that once it knows when and where to look, the agent examines deployments and feature flag changes, then reads the relevant code. It checks when a change actually reached the affected requests and uses logs or traces to test whether the code could explain what happened.

Early on, agents sometimes stopped at the first plausible explanation they found, and some of those diagnoses turned out to be wrong. To catch these mistakes, we added an adversarial review: a separate Codex session that tries to disprove the proposed diagnosis. The reviewer rechecks the assumptions and tests counterfactuals. If a rollout caused the slowdown, did similar requests that weren’t exposed stay healthy? If the suspected change was rolled back, did the affected metric recover?

In one investigation, an agent traced failing ChatGPT conversations to errors in image downloads and marked the cause as found. The Codex reviewer noticed that the internal service responsible for locating files had already recovered while image requests were still failing. The diagnosis did not explain the continuing failures, so the AI reviewer reopened the investigation and recorded what still needed to be established.

Industry observers note that we’ve had success breaking larger jobs into focused Codex turns. In a manual review of 100 root cause suggestions, we graded 70% as accurate, with 30% needing further refinement or not fully establishing causality. In the Regression Workflow, different turns investigate regressions, challenge diagnoses, and propose fixes to increase accuracy numbers through checks and balances.

Once the diagnosis passes adversarial review, the workflow asks Codex to implement a fix and open a pull request. An engineer reviews the PR and decides whether to merge it. We’ve put a significant amount of work into making this handoff as easy as possible. Each task has a report with an automatically generated summary of the regression, its impact, the root cause, and the proposed fix. We’ve tuned these summaries to be easy to scan, including metrics time series, CPU flame graphs, and traces to help engineers promptly understand the findings and inspect the evidence. Engineers can edit the PR directly or use the diagnosis to write their own fix. If they leave comments on the PR, the workflow wakes an agent to address them.

An example task report for a regression reveals key details, root cause, and proposed fix.

According to recent reports, after an engineer deploys the fix, the workflow wakes an agent to check whether performance has returned to its earlier baseline. If it has, the agent marks the task as resolved. If performance has only partially recovered, the agent resolves the original regression and opens a upcoming task for the remaining slowdown, which may have a different cause. If there’s no improvement, the agent records what happened and sends the regression back for investigation.

Getting fixes right has been harder than finding the cause. For example, we’ve seen cases where the agent-proposed changes are more complicated than necessary or introduce fresh issues. Similar to the root cause step, we added an adversarial review of each proposed fix to check whether they address the root cause and help catch bugs or unintended consequences. Some fixes also require higher level architectural decisions. For example, adding a cache might improve performance but introduce stale data. Changes like these benefit from guidance from an engineer who knows the service and can weigh the tradeoffs.

We’re building an evaluation and improvement loop using these cases. By comparing the fixes agents propose with the changes engineers ultimately merge, we can better understand where proposals fall short, build evals, and improve the workflow. We’re also working on using synthetic performance tests so agents can measure proposed fixes and revise them before asking an engineer for review. We’re also exploring how agents could use our other agentic review tools to identify low-risk changes and eventually ship those fixes without a human in the loop.

Building and running the Performance Factory has taught us a lot about developing and operating agent workflows in production. Here are some lessons for teams building their own agentic workflows.

The raw output from a Codex investigation can be a wall of text that’s hard to parse. It takes effort to figure out what the agent is claiming and track down the graphs to see whether the data backs it up. We want engineers to spend their attention on decisions rather than reconstructing the agent’s work.

Sources indicate that agents can investigate more regressions than a team has time to read about. Our first version gave engineers a UI full of findings, but someone still had to decide which information mattered. One regression can also appear as several incidents across alerts, monitors, and channels. The workflow now links related incidents, groups them by the metrics teams care about, and ranks their estimated impact. Engineers can focus on adding context, weighing tradeoffs, and deciding what to ship.

Industry observers note that updating an investigation skill or upgrading the model can make the agent better at diagnosing some cases and worse at others, so we need to test their impact before updating them. We test two things separately: 1) how well the agent investigates and 2) how useful its summaries are to engineers.

For investigations, we backtest against past production incidents. We turn those incidents into a suite of test cases we can rerun when we change the skill. A Codex agent attempts to investigate and resolve the incident, and we compare the agent’s behavior to the actual past resolution data. Each case starts with a fresh Codex investigator and the original signal, stripped of details that might give away the answer.

It has been revealed that historical tests need care. Metrics and traces expire, while evidence collected after recovery can give away the cause. A test is only useful if we understand what evidence the investigator could see. The agent can inspect code and query production telemetry within set limits. It cannot use saved memories (notes from earlier investigations), read the incident writeup, or see results from previous runs. We also inspect its transcript afterward for information that might have spoiled the test.

Recent findings suggest that we score when the problem began, how large it was, and which requests were affected. We also evaluate how the agent uses evidence to rank possible causes and explain what remains uncertain. An agent can get the timing right and still blame the wrong deployment, so we score those separately.

We evaluate task summaries using snapshots of saved tasks. These make particularly good backtests because summarization does not depend on external metrics or traces that expire. A separate grader checks whether an engineer unfamiliar with the system can understand what happened and why it matters, whether useful charts were kept, and whether the proposed next step is supported by the evidence.

According to recent reports, lastly, our agents need monitoring just as much as the services they investigate. A broken profiler or a missing permission can keep an agent from verifying what caused a slowdown. Those failures can be hard to spot in the final report, so we run an agent every day to look through messages and logs from recent runs for tool failures and access errors.

In a recent development, we use the Performance Factory to self-repair and fix the problems this check uncovers. When the same tool error blocks several investigations, the agent creates a task to fix it. If the cause is clear, an agent proposes a fix, and an engineer reviews the change and decides whether to merge it. After merging changes like this, we also use evals to check whether agents can get past the step that previously blocked them.

The Regression Workflow is just one instance of the agent factory pattern that moves tasks through explicit states. Agents advance the task when more work is ready; separate reviewers challenge the conclusions; engineers step in when the next decision requires judgment. Other workflows can reuse the same machinery with different states, instructions, and events.

Sources indicate that from one workflow to many. The Performance Factory can coordinate agents across workflows, with agents in one workflow creating tasks for another.

Right now, our Regression Workflow starts when an alert fires. However, we’re working on more proactive ways for the Performance Factory to find slowdowns and optimizations even when no alert fires. We want agents to use the large amount of fine-grained performance data we already collect to spot regressions our alerts miss or discover optimizations. By comparing different kinds of data (batches of CPU and memory profiles, heap dumps, and request traces across releases), an agent might notice a small increase in CPU for a given request. It can then open a task in the Regression Workflow to trace the increase to its cause, implement a fix, and open a PR for an engineer to review.

In a recent development, in cases where we already know what to look for, we’re working to encode known signals into more Performance Factory workflows. Our service rightsizing skill, for example, helps agents spot autoscaling settings that keep more replicas running than a service needs. When we learn to recognize a pattern like that, we want to build and regularly run a workflow for it across all our services, constantly optimizing in a rapidly changing environment. With the Performance Factory, what an engineer learns from one slowdown can shape how we investigate and fix the next one, even months later in a different service.

According to recent reports, next time you’re using ChatGPT and notice a slowdown, there’s a good chance the Performance Factory is already figuring out why. Today, the bottleneck may be waiting for an engineer to review and merge the fix. We’re already exploring whether agents can do this themselves. As product development keeps accelerating with Codex, performance systems need to become increasingly autonomous and self-improving to keep up. Codex already helps us build ChatGPT faster. Now it’s helping us keep ChatGPT fast.

Special thanks to the team that built the Performance Factory, as well as our post contributors Brendan Gregg, Pieter Hooimeijer, Nick Cooper, and Louis Brandy.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (170 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.27329v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Large instruction-tuning corpora contain substantial semantic redundancy, motivating the selection of compact subsets that preserve useful supervision while reducing training cost. Existing diversity-aware selectors often rely on generated semantic tags and explicit graph structures, introducing considerable annotation and preprocessing overhead. We introduce H-MSAE, a hierarchical sparse instruction selection framework that organizes multi-resolution concepts learned by a Matryoshka sparse autoencoder into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. Quality-weighted, diminishing-return coverage with ancestor propagation promotes high-quality and non-redundant semantic coverage, while pool-relative length constraints regulate subset composition. We motivate this design through a local quality-diversity analysis of subset SFT utility and examine it using example-quality and representation-space diversity diagnostics. On Tulu 3 data pool, H-MSAE achieves the highest Final Avg among the evaluated 50K selectors across scales and initialization. The selected subset also exhibits the highest mean quality and effective rank among the evaluated methods. By avoiding full-pool generative tagging and supporting efficient sparse selection, H-MSAE reduces measured end-to-end runtime by approximately $5\times$ relative to MIG.

Amazon CloudFront adds IP based routing and connection logs to SaaS Manager

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (251 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon CloudFront now allows web development and SaaS platforms to serve different tiers of customers on the same wildcard domain by using IP addresses to route them to the right configuration.
  • Previously, CloudFront chose the configuration from the domain name alone, so the same domain always went to the same configuration.
  • According to recent reports, these features are available at all CloudFront edge locations.

Amazon CloudFront now allows web development and SaaS platforms to serve different tiers of customers on the same wildcard domain by using IP addresses to route them to the right configuration. For example, these platforms can serve premium and pro customers from dedicated Anycast static IP address lists, each with its own configuration, and serve free-tier customers on the shared CloudFront IP addresses, all under *.example.com. Additionally, these customers also have visibility into viewer connections with connection logging.

Previously, CloudFront chose the configuration from the domain name alone, so the same domain always went to the same configuration. With address-based selection, you can register the same wildcard domain on several IP lists and send each list to its own tenant. Because you control which clients resolve to which IP list, you can shift traffic between your service tiers without your customers needing to make any changes. You can also serve IoT devices, embedded SDKs, and older TLS clients that connect by IP address without sending a domain name in the TLS handshake (Server Name Indication, or SNI). With viewer fallback, you choose a distribution to accept these connections, and CloudFront uses the Host header in each request to serve the right content. Connection logs now also record HTTPS connections to these tenants which helps you troubleshoot how clients connect.

According to recent reports, these features are available at all CloudFront edge locations. To learn more, see Address-based selection and Connection Logs in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

In a recent development, running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a massive part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

In a recent development, this is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so consumers can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

Industry observers note that we want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

Recent findings suggest that GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

In a recent development, we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

According to recent reports, that is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

In a recent development, the model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

Industry observers note that for models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

According to recent reports, transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

It has been revealed that our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

It has been revealed that the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

Sources indicate that llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

Sources indicate that transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for fresh architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

According to recent reports, that opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

According to recent reports, our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

It has been revealed that A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

According to recent reports, to show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Recent findings suggest that faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

It has been revealed that these changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

Industry observers note that if you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an problem with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.
